title: Steak Tartare
subtitle: Hand-chopped raw beef with egg yolk and capers
excerpt: This is a dish that relies on sourcing. Buy the best, freshest sirloin you can find and keep it cold until the moment you chop it. Raw beef and raw egg carry food safety risk; serve immediately after preparation and do not make for vulnerable groups.
sourceNotes: Steak tartare appears in French haute cuisine from at least the early twentieth century, though its name's connection to Tartar tribes is largely apocryphal. The dish depends entirely on the quality and freshness of the beef, which must be hand-chopped rather than minced for the right texture.

content.text: Chop the beef with a sharp knife rather than processing it -- a food processor turns it to paste. The finished texture should be rough and slightly chunky, not smooth. The raw egg yolk goes on top and is mixed in at the table.

items.prepNote: very fresh, centre-cut, all sinew removed, hand-chopped to a coarse mince

content.text: Keep the beef well-chilled until needed. Remove any sinew or fat, then chop with a sharp knife to a coarse, uneven mince. Do not overwork it.
In a bowl, combine the chopped beef with the dijon mustard, capers, red wine vinegar, olive oil, and most of the chives. Mix briefly with a fork. Taste for seasoning and adjust.
Divide between two chilled plates, pressing into a round mould or shaping with a spoon. Make a small indent in the centre of each portion.
Place an egg yolk in each indent. Scatter the remaining chives over the top. Serve immediately with toasted bread on the side.

items.cause: Chopped too fine or too warm.
items.fix: Keep the meat cold throughout and use the tip of the knife to rough-chop rather than a rocking motion that over-processes.
